analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators order refunds of excessive market-based electricity rates, with interest.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it drew no cosponsors and died without a vote when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government had allowed much of the wholesale electricity market to be sold at market-based prices rather than regulated rates, and federal regulators had limited power to claw back charges that turned out too high. This bill would have let the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order refunds of the portion of market-based electricity charges it found unjust, unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory, including interest, going back up to two years. It was introduced in the final weeks of the 106th Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity customers, especially those buying power in regions where market-based wholesale prices spiked, would gain a way to recover overcharges. If a seller charged more than a just and reasonable rate, the commission could order that excess refunded with interest.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Power Act so the commission can order refunds of the portion of market-based rates and charges it finds exceed a just, reasonable, and non-discriminatory rate, with interest from the date the charge was paid.

It applies specifically to rates sold under commission rules or orders allowing market-based prices, closing a gap where charges set by market authority were harder to claw back than traditionally regulated rates.
Customers could trigger review by complaint, not only by the commission acting on its own motion.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers operating under market-based rate authority — generators and power marketers — would bear the cost of refunds of excessive charges plus interest, and would face greater uncertainty that past charges could be clawed back.

drawbacks.text: The refund window is limited: no refund could reach amounts paid more than two years before the commission's notice was published, so older overcharges would remain unrecoverable.
The bill also bars certain retroactive refunds and applies only to complaints filed after August 1, 2000, limiting how far back it would reach even at enactment.

A fair objection from sellers: the threat of retroactive refunds, with interest, adds financial risk to market-based sales, which sellers argued could raise the cost or reduce the willingness to invest in power supplies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, consumer-side fix: it targets only charges above a just and reasonable rate, caps the lookback at two years, and preserves all existing authority. Its main cost falls on sellers who may have collected above-market charges. The larger limitation is design and timing — it arrived with no cosponsors in the final weeks of a Congress, so its consumer protections never got any test.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, sat there with no hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the bill on November 3, 2000, near the end of the 106th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day, and on November 8, 2000 to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No further action was taken; the bill drew no cosponsors and received no hearing or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers operating under market-based rate authority were better off, since they faced no risk of commission-ordered refunds of past charges. Electricity customers received no avenue to recover excessive market-based charges.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers kept their charges

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give federal regulators refund authority over market-based electricity rates.

against.name: Rep. Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Committee leadership never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee and then subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no party split ever formed; it was a single Democrat's late-session proposal.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers (generators and power marketers under market-based rate authority)
industries.note: The bill would have let regulators order refunds, with interest, of charges found to exceed a just and reasonable rate. Sellers charging market-based prices bore the cost; the public benefit was recovering overcharges.

The bill would have expanded the commission's refund authority over market-based rates while removing the general refund provision of section 206(b) for those rates and adding a two-year lookback limit.
